rule: Use diverging bars for survey results involving sentiment like disagree, neutral, agree.
quote: Perfect for presenting survey results which involve sentiment (eg disagree/neutral/agree).

rule: Use ordered bars or columns to show ranks more easily than unsorted charts.
quote: Standard bar charts display the ranks of values much more easily when sorted into order

rule: Keep gaps between columns small in histograms to highlight the shape of data distribution.
quote: The standard way to show a statistical distribution - keep the gaps between columns small to highlight the 'shape' of the data

rule: Warn readers when data relationships may appear causal unless explicitly stated otherwise.
quote: Be mindful that, unless you tell them otherwise, many readers will assume the relationships you show them to be causal (i.e. one causes the other).

rule: Always start numerical axes at zero for part-to-whole and comparison charts like bar and area charts.
quote: Always start numerical axes at zero for part-to-whole and comparisons charts, such as bar and area chart.

rule: Never interpolate between periods when data is unavailable; label both start and end points of data gaps.
quote: Never interpolate between periods when data is unavailable. Always label both the start and end point during which data is not available.

rule: Use a sinusoidal line to mark axis breaks instead of a straight axis line.
quote: When the axis contains a break, use a sinusoidal line to replace the straight axis line.

rule: Never change axis tick increments to accommodate data availability; use axis break styling instead.
quote: Never change axis ticks increments to accommodate data availability. If any form of axis compression is required, use the provided axis break styling to visually denote the compression.

rule: Use localized date and time formats in time-series X-axis labels when possible, reflecting user preference.
quote: When possible, use localized date and time format, or user preference. Otherwise, the chart defaults to the format presented below.

rule: Semibold labels when data crosses into a new time cycle (day, month, year) to create landmark context.
quote: Whenever data crosses into a new time cycle, such as a new day, month, or year, semibold the label to make it a "landmark" label to provide additional context for the labels following it.

rule: Apply categorical palette colors in sequence strictly as described to maximize contrast between neighboring colors.
quote: The colors of this palette should be applied in sequence strictly as described below. The sequence is carefully curated to maximize contrast between neighboring colors to help with visual differentiation.

rule: Never use gradients in place of sequential palettes; use gradients only to highlight extremes in single-category visualizations.
quote: Gradients should not be used to represent any meaningful progression or divergence. Never use a gradient in place of a sequential palette.

rule: Make chart titles descriptive and qualitative, reflecting the main insight the data reveals.
quote: The title of a piece of visualization should be descriptive and qualitative. It should also reflect the main insight the data reveals.

rule: Use labels directly on charts to avoid long legends when possible.
quote: When possible, use labels directly on the chart to avoid long legends.

rule: Keep all chart text concise and easy to understand.
quote: All the text should be concise and easy to understand.

rule: Tooltips should repeat corresponding values on both axes and any other relevant details for data points.
quote: A tooltip should repeat the corresponding values of the data point on both axes and any other relevant details.

rule: Avoid filling the chart frame with too many elements, as it impacts the user's ability to interpret data.
quote: Avoid filling the chart frame with too many elements, as it impacts the user's ability to interpret the data.

rule: Use a callout to clearly associate a label with a slice when the graphic translation is less than 3 degrees.
quote: When the graphic translation of the data is less than 3 degrees, a callout is used to clearly associate the label with the slice.

rule: Use sequential scales with all positive or all negative values in heat maps.
quote: It's best practice to use a sequential scale with values that are all positive or all negative.

rule: Leverage the full range of the palette (from 10–100) in sequential heat maps to maximize contrast.
quote: Sequential heat maps can leverage the full range of the palette (from 10–100) to maximize contrast.

rule: Use three colors for divergent heat map scales corresponding to min, max, and inflection point values.
quote: Divergent scales require three colors for their correspondent values (min, max, and inflection point) and Carbon has provided two approved palettes for divergent visualizations.

rule: Default inflection point to zero in divergent heat maps to accommodate the most common cases.
quote: We default to zero in order to accommodate the most common cases and include a feature flag within the code to specify exceptions.

rule: Include zoom functionality in Circle Packs with more than two levels of hierarchy to let users explore data without sacrificing contrast.
quote: For Circle Packs with more than two levels of hierarchy, zoom functionality allows users to explore the data without compromising the contrast accessibility of the chart.

rule: Use different color sets for each block in multi-block alluvial diagrams to emphasize non-correlated connections.
quote: This is usually emphasized using a different set of colors for each block.

rule: Use floating zoom and pan controls in network diagrams to enable simultaneous zooming and panning.
quote: Network diagrams use the same scale controls that apply to the rest of the data visualization components, however they appear in a floating tile, enabling the user to zoom and pan simultaneously.

rule: Include expand and collapse all nodes feature in network diagrams for easy navigation between detailed and high-level views.
quote: It's also helpful to include the expand and collapse all nodes feature, which gives users the ability to easily navigate between detailed and high-level views of the diagram.

rule: Use hover effects to highlight specific groups or axes in parallel coordinate charts to enhance comprehension.
quote: Hover effects that highlight a specific group or axis can be added to enhance basic parallel coordinate charts.

rule: Use dendrograms instead of tree diagrams when layouts must respond to varying screen sizes.
quote: Although the two are very similar, dendrograms tend to offer a more responsive layout for varying screen sizes.

rule: Use stacked area and bar charts to compare proportional contributions within categories.
quote: Stacked charts are useful for comparing proportional contributions within a category. They plot the relative value that each data series contributes to the total.

rule: Use bar charts to compare discrete data or show trends over time.
quote: Bar charts use vertical or horizontal data markers to compare individual values. You can use them to compare discrete data or show trends over time.

rule: Use bubble charts to represent financial data or related measured values on two axes with size as a third measure.
quote: You can use bubble charts to represent financial data or any data where measured values are related.

rule: Use line charts to show trends over time and compare several data sets.
quote: You can use line visualizations to show trends over time and compare several data sets.

rule: Use scatter plots to explore correlations between different measures.
quote: You can use scatter plots to explore correlations between different measures.

rule: Use stepped line charts to show trends over time with discrete intervals between data points.
quote: Stepped line charts plot data at regular intervals, forming a series of steps between data points. You can use line visualizations to show trends over time and compare several data sets.

rule: Use tree maps for visualizing part-to-whole relationships when hierarchical data must fit constrained space.
quote: Tree maps can work for visualizing a part-to-whole relationship among a large number of categories—as long as the data is hierarchical and exact comparisons between the categories is not a primary concern.

rule: Prefer Circle Packs over Tree Maps when revealing hierarchical structure is more important than space efficiency.
quote: Although they're not as space efficient, Circle Packs reveal hierarchical structure better than Treemaps.

rule: Use motion to identify the next step, inform people of changes, and celebrate accomplishments.
quote: Use motion to identify the next step, inform people of changes in the UI, and celebrate what they've accomplished.

rule: Design motion following physical laws like inertia, gravity, weight, and velocity to feel fluid and believable.
quote: Motion in Fluent 2 experiences feels fluid and real by following physical laws such as inertia, gravity, weight and velocity.

rule: Make animation duration proportional to element size; give larger elements more time to animate.
quote: Give larger elements more time to animate than smaller elements. Aim for a fast and smooth motion without making people wait.

rule: Use ease-in-out animations to start slow, speed up in the middle, then slow down again.
quote: Ease-in-out animations start slow, speed up in the middle, and then slow down again before ending.

rule: Visually connect elements that change position and size from one state to another to lower cognitive load.
quote: Elements that change position and size should visually connect from one state to another, even if they aren't connected under the hood.

rule: Make surfaces sharing the same UI entry point invoke and dismiss the same way for consistency.
quote: Surfaces that share the same UI entry point should invoke and dismiss the same way to bring consistency to interactions.

rule: Use page transitions to guide user eyes to incoming and outgoing content, lowering cognitive load.
quote: Page transitions guide your user's eyes to incoming and outgoing content, lowering cognitive load.

rule: Use productive motion for tasks requiring focus; reserve expressive motion for important occasional moments.
quote: Reserve expressive motion for occasional, important moments, to better capture the user's attention and offer a rhythmic break to the productive experience.

rule: Apply easing curves so elements speed up quickly and slow down smoothly, obeying light-weight material physics.
quote: Elements on the screen should speed up quickly and slow down smoothly, obeying the physics of a light-weight material.

rule: Scale motion duration based on animation size; larger changes require longer animation times.
quote: Motion's duration should be dynamic based on the size of the animation; the larger the change in distance (traveled) or size (scaling) of the element, the longer the animation takes.

rule: Avoid easing curves that are unnatural, distracting, or purely decorative in motion design.
quote: Avoid easing curves that are unnatural, distracting, or purely decorative. IBM motion is essential and efficient, guiding users to value as quickly as possible.

rule: Animate elements along grid paths only; never use diagonal motion paths.
quote: Motion paths trace lines along the grid which never run diagonally.

rule: Use identical motion for elements that convey the same meaning or perform the same function.
quote: When elements convey the same meaning or perform the same function, use the same motion for them, and vice-versa.

rule: Stagger entrance animations by 20ms increments; keep total animation time under 500ms to reduce cognitive load.
quote: staggering the entrance of table content by 20 ms significantly reduces the cognitive load. Depending on the number of staggered elements, the delay should be adjusted to ensure that total time is still within 500 ms.
finding: 20ms stagger reduces cognitive load; total time must stay under 500ms

rule: Design motion as temporal composition over time, not static states; principles must address property changes over time.
quote: when you're talking about interface animation principles you're talking about design in time. It's not just speaking to the composition of how these objects perform in time, but you're speaking to what are

rule: Test interfaces in color vision deficiency modes to ensure distinguishability of red, green, and yellow hues.
quote: In this mode, it is difficult to distinguish hues of green, red, and yellow from one another.

rule: Lazy load SVG animations to reduce First Contentful Paint and improve perceived page responsiveness.
quote: Multiple SVG animations on a page can slow down First Contentful Paint (FCP) because the browser needs to evaluate all JavaScript before rendering.

rule: Use CSS animations for simple hover or load effects because CSS rendering uses GPU and is faster than JavaScript animations.
quote: CSS animations use the GPU for rendering, which makes them faster and more efficient.

rule: Extract JavaScript from SVG files and load it only after page render completes to improve First Contentful Paint.
quote: You can optimize this by not loading the JavaScript from SVGs until the page is fully loaded. To do this, extract the script tags from inside the SVG, place the JavaScript in an external file, and set it to load when a specific event triggers.

rule: Load the SVG animation player from a CDN and cache it globally; reuse one cached player across multiple animations.
quote: When multiple SVGs use the external player, it is downloaded only once and used by all animations. This is much faster than embedding the player in every SVG file.

rule: Use desaturated, very bright or very dark background colors in data visualizations.
quote: Your background color should be desaturated, and either very bright or very dark.

rule: Use the same color if chart elements are already distinguished by another visual variable like position.
quote: Consider giving elements in your chart the same color if they're already distinguished by another visual variable.

rule: Use shades of one hue instead of different hues to reduce visual clutter.
quote: Consider coloring categories in darker and lighter versions of the same hue instead of in different hues.

rule: Emphasize only the most important categories with color to guide reader focus.
quote: there are always more and less important points you want to make — and therefore categories you can emphasize visually, while letting other categories recede into the background.

rule: Use color as the primary tool to direct reader attention across a visualization.
quote: One of the biggest superpowers of colors might be to lead a reader's eye. By emphasizing certain data points and de-emphasizing others, you can decide what you want readers to see first, second, third, and last.

rule: Use more saturated colors for important categories and desaturate less important ones.
quote: Use more saturated colors for more important categories

rule: Design color keys to help readers quickly understand what colored elements in visualizations mean.
quote: The goal of a color key — also called a color legend — is to help your reader figure out as quickly as possible what the colored elements in your visualization mean.

rule: Use direct labels instead of color keys when possible to reduce cognitive load.
quote: Your readers won't know what a color indicates if you don't explain it to them. But that explanation doesn't need to happen in the form of a key. You might be able to use direct labels instead

rule: Create a fixed color palette for data visualizations to build brand trust and consistency.
quote: Consistent colors will help to build a brand and hence more trust. Readers will know they can trust a chart — no matter where it appears — when it looks like it comes from you.

rule: Start with 3-10 colors for a basic data visualization palette using brand or website colors.
quote: Choose 3-10 different colors. These can be your logo color(s), or colors from your website
finding: YouGov found they could complete 90% of simple charts with a limited palette

rule: Use CSS animations for simple, declarative effects requiring browser optimization and hardware acceleration.
quote: CSS animations excel for simple, declarative animations that leverage browser optimization. They're ideal for hover effects, loading spinners, and basic state transitions.

rule: Choose JavaScript libraries like GSAP for complex animations requiring timeline control, dynamic values, or physics-based effects.
quote: Choose JavaScript libraries when CSS limitations become apparent—typically for timeline control, dynamic values, or physics-based animations.

rule: Respect prefers-reduced-motion to ensure animations are accessible to users sensitive to motion.
quote: Always check for reduced motion preferences: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)

rule: Use SVG filters judiciously; they impact performance more than transforms or opacity changes.
quote: Use filters judiciously—they impact performance more than transforms or opacity changes.

rule: Use subtle animation that supports content rather than competing with it for a more professional experience.
quote: Animation should support content—not compete with it. Subtle movement often creates a more professional experience than constant motion.

rule: Guide readers through non-standard chart types with annotations and clear axis labels explaining how to interact.
quote: As these improvised scatter-type charts are a little different, we try to make sure we guide the reader through it as best we can: offering instruction to hover or select in the standfirst, where appropriate, and using annotations to explain how the axes work.

rule: Place titles near their related charts; position legends close to charts they serve; position filters adjacent to charts they influence.
quote: Titles should be placed near the charts they are related to. Color keys (legends) need to be located close to the charts they are used in. Filters/parameters (and other settings) should be positioned closer to the charts they influence.

rule: Use color to group similar elements and direct attention, not as decoration without semantic meaning.
quote: Use color efficiently to enhance navigation and perception of your visualizations. If the chart is merely colored without carrying any semantic meaning, it may be harder to interpret than if left without color altogether.

rule: Sort and order chart elements for continuity: bars largest to smallest, time series past to future.
quote: Bar charts are more comprehensible when arranged from larger to smaller, time charts from past to future, and so forth. This organization allows us to perceive them as one continuous whole.

rule: Users parse layouts in a fraction of a second before reading labels; ensure proximity, borders, alignment, color, and motion match content grouping.
quote: Users parse a layout before they read its labels. Whitespace, borders, alignment, color, and motion determine what belongs together. When these cues fight the content, users attach the label, price, warning, status, or action to the wrong object.

rule: Perceptual objects must match interaction objects: if a card looks selectable as one unit, all its contents should respond together.
quote: Perceptual objects should match interaction objects. If a card looks like one selectable unit but only its title is clickable, the interface contradicts itself.

rule: Reserve whitespace to separate visual chunks; dense layouts trigger grouping collapse where all elements cluster together.
quote: Proximity also explains why cramming a dense form into a tight space backfires. Squeeze everything together and you trigger a grouping collapse: every element clusters with every other element, which is the same as no grouping at all. Whitespace isn't wasted space. It's the mortar that holds your visual chunks apart.

rule: Use color similarity for buttons and interactive elements so users learn to treat matching visuals as interactive.
quote: In a well-built interface, clickable buttons share the same color and shape. Users quickly learn to treat anything that looks that way as interactive.

rule: Aim for 60 frames per second to match device refresh rates; animations below this appear stuttered and erratic.
quote: Good performance means hitting the ultimate goal of 60 frames per second (FPS). That's because most devices these days refresh their screen at a rate of 60 times a second. The browser needs to match this rate and paint a new frame on each refresh.
finding: 60 FPS required to match device refresh rate

rule: Use ease-out for elements entering the screen; they arrive fast and settle gently, feeling responsive.
quote: My advice: use ease-out for elements entering the screen. They arrive fast and settle gently, which feels responsive.

rule: Use ease-in for elements leaving the screen and ease-in-out for elements moving between locations.
quote: Use ease-in for elements leaving, and ease-in-out for elements that move from one place to another.

rule: Reserve linear easing for genuinely mechanical elements: loading spinners, marquees, progress bars.
quote: Reserve linear for things that genuinely are mechanical: loading spinners, marquees, progress bars.

rule: Limit categorical data visualization colors to 5-6 maximum; group additional categories together.
quote: Limit the number of colors presented in your data visualization to 5-6 by grouping additional categories together.

rule: Apply visual separators between adjacent chart colors to meet accessibility contrast requirements.
quote: Apply a space or border ( color.border.inverse ) as a visual separator between data elements.

rule: Use visual indicators beyond color alone—shapes, patterns, or direct labels—to communicate meaning in data.
quote: Incorporate visual indicators other than color into your data visualization.

rule: Keep gaps between histogram columns small to highlight the shape of the data distribution.
quote: keep the gaps between columns small to highlight the 'shape' of the data

rule: Warn readers when data relationships may appear causal unless explicitly stated otherwise.
quote: Be mindful that, unless you tell them otherwise, many readers will assume the relationships you show them to be causal

rule: In sequential heat maps, use values that are all positive or all negative to maximize readability of the color progression.
quote: It's best practice to use a sequential scale with values that are all positive or all negative

rule: Leverage the full range of the heat map color palette (10–100) in sequential scales to maximize contrast between values.
quote: Sequential heat maps can leverage the full range of the palette (from 10–100) to maximize contrast

rule: In divergent heat maps, default the inflection point to zero to accommodate the most common use cases of balanced scales.
quote: We default to zero in order to accommodate the most common cases and include a feature flag within the code to specify exceptions

rule: Include zoom functionality in Circle Packs with more than two levels of hierarchy to let users explore data without sacrificing contrast accessibility.
quote: For Circle Packs with more than two levels of hierarchy, zoom functionality allows users to explore the data without compromising the contrast accessibility of the chart

rule: Prefer Circle Packs over Tree Maps when revealing hierarchical structure is more important than space efficiency.
quote: Although they're not as space efficient, Circle Packs reveal hierarchical structure better than Treemaps

rule: Use staggered animation with short offsets to soften entry of large item sets and guide visual attention.
quote: Staggering is the process of delaying the start of one or more animations. This can be used to soften the entry of large sets of items or to shift people's gaze in a specified direction.

rule: Constrain motion to elements in focus; avoid adding motion elsewhere on screen to prevent distraction from the user's task.
quote: Keep the motion constrained to the element in focus. Adding motion in other areas of the screen may distract from the task at hand.

rule: Use exit easing to speed up elements as they exit view, implying permanent departure; use standard easing if elements stay nearby ready to reappear.
quote: Use exit-easing when removing elements from view, such as closing a modal or toaster. The element speeds up as it exits from view, implying that its departure from the screen is permanent.

rule: Keep micro-interaction motion between 90–120 milliseconds and use ease-out on user input for responsive feedback.
quote: Do micro-interactions use ease-out on user input? Do micro-interactions fall within a static duration ranging from 90–120 ms?

rule: Use spring physics for animations where motion quality matters most; avoid springs for color or opacity changes.
quote: Springs are most impactful when it comes to motion; I wouldn't use them for color or opacity changes.

rule: Use warm, desaturated, very bright background colors in data visualizations for reliable contrast and legibility.
quote: If you want to be sure, use a warm, very bright, desaturated background color.
finding: Most advanced data vis designers used warm backgrounds like yellow or orange; the blue backgrounds used by The Economist were noted as outliers.

rule: Vary chart types within a story to maintain reader attention and show data more accurately than repeating one type.
quote: Repetitive chart types, even when they're nicely designed, don't attract readers' attention

rule: Prioritize chart content relevance over novelty; interesting data in simple formats outperforms complex visualizations with dull data.
quote: Simple charts are not boring when they show interesting data

rule: Space form fields closer to their labels than to adjacent fields; equidistant gaps cause roughly 50% of users to pair them incorrectly.
quote: when labels sit equidistant between two fields, they land in label limbo: users guess, and roughly half of them guess wrong
finding: 50% error rate with equidistant label spacing

rule: Test visual grouping at narrow breakpoints, maximum text sizes, longest content, and all error or loading states; ideal screenshots alone do not confirm correct grouping.
quote: A layout that groups correctly only in the ideal screenshot is not correctly grouped

rule: Animate only transform and opacity properties to avoid triggering layout or paint; all other property animations force expensive rendering work.
quote: the most performant way to animate is with CSS keyframe animations or transitions on transform and opacity only

rule: Apply will-change sparingly only to elements that animate often; overuse creates memory overhead that negates GPU benefits.
quote: will-change is a powerful tool that should only be used sparingly. It is absolutely not recommended to put every element onto its own layer

rule: Defer JavaScript execution from SVGs until after page render completes to improve First Contentful Paint.
quote: extract the script tags from inside the SVG, place the JavaScript in an external file, and set it to load when a specific event triggers

rule: Reduce SVG file size by 30% using SVGO optimization before animating to lower bandwidth and load time.
quote: We've managed to reduce SVG file size by about 30% with this tool, though results vary depending on how well-formed the SVG already is.

rule: Reserve space for lazy-loaded SVGs by setting width and height on the container to prevent layout shift.
quote: Make sure to set the width and height of the object element to match the SVG dimensions. This way, the browser reserves the correct space for the SVG and prevents content from shifting when it renders.

rule: Respect prefers-reduced-motion media queries to disable animations for users sensitive to motion.
quote: Always check for reduced motion preferences

rule: Split multi-category charts into small multiples instead of cramming all categories into one chart.
quote: Can you split the categories into multiple charts?

rule: Use stroke width, dashes, patterns, or symbols to distinguish categories instead of relying solely on color.
quote: Can you add symbols, patterns, line widths, or dashes?

rule: Use white strokes around same-colored chart elements to separate them visually without adding new colors.
quote: The white stroke around each line makes them easier to follow, especially where same-colored lines overlap.

rule: Make de-emphasized categories gray or use desaturated versions of the highlight color, never a new hue.
quote: Don't use new hues for deemphasized categories. To be on the safe side, stick to gray or desaturation for de-emphasized categories.

rule: Arrange color key items in a grid layout when the key has many items or long labels to improve scannability.
quote: If your key has lots of items, or you need a lot of letters to describe them, it can become overwhelming. If this is the case, consider using a grid layout — it's easier to skim and looks tidier.

rule: Show form (line thickness, dashes, patterns, strokes) alongside color in legends to help readers match visual elements.
quote: If your colored elements have different forms (thick lines, thin lines, dashed lines, rectangles…), then showing these forms in the color key is an excellent way to help readers quickly find them in the chart.

rule: Organize color palette order and primary colors to reduce designer decisions and speed up chart creation.
quote: Keeping the order of colours in the palette consistent helps non-designers create basic charts in a fast-paced environment without having to spend time on yet another design decision

rule: Define primary colors explicitly; most organizations complete 90% of simple charts with only a few core hues.
quote: We find we can get 90% of our simple charts done with this simple palette.
finding: 90% of simple charts completed with limited palette

rule: Use few hues with multiple shades for brand recognition; designers recognize this style instantly after one exposure.
quote: Brand recognition through these colors is crazy high. It's basically through the roof. You can't do better.

rule: Avoid color meanings that conflict with topic; use mixed or desaturated colors when unsure of cultural associations.
quote: Be appropriate for the topic and evoke the right associations — or none at all. You might want to avoid intense reds ('Danger!'), grass green ('Good')

rule: Respect the prefers-reduced-motion media feature to support users who prefer reduced motion in animations.
quote: Support users who prefer reduced motion by respecting the prefers-reduced-motion media feature.
